891.event_title: Japan destroys the Russian fleet at Tsushima
891.place: Tsushima Strait, between Korea and Japan
891.event: During the Russo-Japanese War, Russia sent its Baltic Fleet on a voyage of nearly 20,000 nautical miles to the Far East. In the Tsushima Strait the Japanese fleet under Admiral Togo Heihachiro crossed the Russian line of advance and destroyed or captured almost the entire Russian force. Britannica describes it as the first occasion in the modern era on which an Asian power defeated a European nation, and Russia soon accepted peace in the Treaty of Portsmouth.
891.explanation: A great European empire that had treated Japan as a minor power was decisively defeated by it, changing how the world saw Japan.
891.tie_back: The kural says the first safeguard is never to belittle the strength of those able to carry out what they undertake, a lesson Russia learned at Tsushima.
891._accuracy_note: A good illustration of the cost of underrating a capable opponent; the sources document the defeat, while Russian underestimation is a historians' interpretation kept out of the event field.

892.event_title: Einstein signs the letter warning Roosevelt about atomic bombs
892.place: Long Island, New York, United States
892.event: Albert Einstein left Germany after the Nazis came to power in 1933 and settled in the United States, and the Hungarian-born physicist Leo Szilard also left Germany in 1933 because of rising anti-Semitism. In 1939, fearing that Germany might build an atomic bomb, Szilard drafted a letter dated 2 August 1939 that Einstein signed, warning President Franklin D. Roosevelt that uranium fission could lead to extremely powerful bombs. Delivered by Alexander Sachs in October, the letter led Roosevelt to set up the Advisory Committee on Uranium, a step towards the Manhattan Project.
892.explanation: Scientists whom Nazi Germany had driven out played a key part in starting the effort that gave its enemies the decisive weapon of the war.
892.tie_back: The kural warns that disregarding the great brings lasting trouble at their hands, and Germany's treatment of its own scientists turned their talents to the service of its foes.
892._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: the trouble came from the great whom Germany disregarded, but Einstein himself took no part in building the bomb.

893.event_title: Iraq ignores the UN deadline to leave Kuwait
893.event: Iraqi forces invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, and the UN Security Council at once demanded their immediate and unconditional withdrawal, then imposed sanctions. In November 1990 Resolution 678 authorized member states to use all necessary means unless Iraq withdrew by 15 January 1991. Iraq did not withdraw, and a coalition of forces from more than 30 nations began air attacks on 16-17 January and a ground offensive on 24 February that liberated Kuwait within about four days.
893.explanation: Iraq's leadership defied repeated warnings from a coalition with overwhelming power and saw its army driven out of Kuwait in days.
893.tie_back: The kural says that one who wants ruin need only offend, without heeding anyone, those able to destroy whenever they wish, which Iraq did by ignoring every warning.
893._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of defying a power able to destroy despite repeated warnings; the invasion itself is described only in outline.

894.event: When the Sultan of Zanzibar died on 25 August 1896, Khalid ibn Barghash seized the palace and proclaimed himself sultan against the wishes of Britain, which had declared a protectorate over Zanzibar. Britain issued an ultimatum to stand down by 9 am on 27 August, and when Khalid refused, British warships bombarded the palace. The war was over in under an hour, the shortest on record; Khalid fled to the German consulate and Britain installed its own candidate as sultan.
894.explanation: A ruler with a handful of guns defied the strongest navy in the world and lost everything in less than an hour.
894.tie_back: The kural says that when the powerless provoke the powerful it is like beckoning Death with one's own hand, as Khalid's defiance of the Royal Navy shows.
894._accuracy_note: A very close illustration of the weak provoking the strong to their own swift ruin, though Britain itself was acting as an imperial power, not an innocent party.

895.place: Carthage, Ephesus and Bithynia (present-day Tunisia and Turkey)
895.event: After his defeat at Zama, Hannibal was denounced to Rome by rivals in Carthage and fled in 195 BCE to the court of Antiochus III. When Rome defeated Antiochus, one of its peace terms was that Hannibal be surrendered, and he fled again, eventually taking refuge with King Prusias of Bithynia. When the Romans demanded him there too, he took poison at Libyssa around 183 BCE rather than be handed over.
895.explanation: For more than a decade Rome's enmity followed Hannibal from one kingdom to the next until no refuge remained.
895.tie_back: The kural says those who earn the wrath of a fiercely strong power will not survive wherever they flee, which matches Hannibal's last years.
895._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the inescapable reach of a powerful enemy's anger, though the pursuer was the Roman Republic rather than a king, and Hannibal was Rome's enemy rather than a subject who offended it.

896.event_title: Galileo is tried by the Inquisition
896.event: In 1624 Pope Urban VIII allowed Galileo to write about systems of the universe on condition that the Copernican theory be treated only as a hypothesis. Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, published in 1632, did not do so, and the pope convened a commission that found he had disobeyed a 1616 injunction. Tried by the Inquisition in 1633, Galileo was condemned, the Dialogue was banned, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest near Florence until his death in 1642.
896.explanation: Even the most famous scientist in Europe could not escape the consequences of crossing the conditions set by the most powerful authority of his world.
896.tie_back: The kural says one may survive a fire but not the anger of the great one has offended, and Galileo, though spared harsher punishment, never regained his freedom.
896._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows the consequence of displeasing a great power, but Galileo is remembered as in the right, which runs against the kural's moral frame of offending the worthy.

897.event_title: Ida Tarbell's exposé and the break-up of Standard Oil
897.place: New York and Washington, D.C., United States
897.event: From November 1902 to October 1904 the journalist Ida Tarbell published a 19-part series in McClure's Magazine documenting the unfair tactics and railroad rebates through which John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil had come to control nearly all oil refining and marketing in the United States. The federal government brought an antitrust suit against the company, and in May 1911 the Supreme Court ordered the Standard Oil trust dissolved, splitting it into 34 independent companies. The Library of Congress and Britannica both credit Tarbell's reporting as a major influence on the outcome.
897.explanation: The richest business in the world could not protect itself once a determined, principled investigator had laid out the truth before the public and the courts.
897.tie_back: The kural asks what use splendid wealth is once the truly worthy turn against its holder, and Standard Oil's vast fortune did not save the trust.
897._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of moral authority prevailing over great wealth, though the decisive act was the government's lawsuit rather than Tarbell's anger alone.

898.event: In October 1911 a revolt broke out in Wuchang (Wuhan) and spread across China, and the revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen was chosen as provisional president of the new republic. On 12 February 1912 the six-year-old emperor Puyi was forced to abdicate, ending 267 years of Qing rule and China's imperial system of some 2,000 years. Under the settlement Sun handed the presidency to Yuan Shikai, and Puyi was allowed to live on in the palace.
898.explanation: A dynasty that had ruled China for centuries and seemed permanent fell within months once the revolution gathered strength.
898.tie_back: The kural says that even those who seem permanently established will perish together with their lineage when the mountain-like great resolve against them, and the Qing dynasty fell along with the imperial system itself.
898._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows a seemingly permanent dynasty falling, but the revolution was a broad movement rather than the anger of particular great persons the kural describes.

899.event: In 1688 King James II ordered his Declaration of Indulgence to be read in churches, and the Archbishop of Canterbury and six other bishops petitioned him to withdraw the order, arguing that the royal power to suspend laws on which it rested was illegal. The king had them imprisoned in the Tower and tried for seditious libel, but on 30 June 1688 a jury acquitted them amid public celebration. That same day seven leading Englishmen invited William of Orange to intervene, and by the end of the year William had landed and James had fled the country.
899.explanation: By prosecuting the bishops, the king turned respected men of principle into public heroes and lost the confidence of the nation within months.
899.tie_back: The kural says that when those of lofty principle are roused, even a king is broken midway and loses his kingdom, which describes James II's fall in 1688.
899._accuracy_note: A very close fit for a king undone after confronting men of principle, though his fall also had other causes, notably the birth of his son and William's own plans.

900.event_title: Syngman Rhee resigns after the April Revolution
900.event: After government claims that South Korea's March 1960 election had given President Syngman Rhee more than 90 percent of the vote, student protests against electoral fraud spread across the country, culminating in mass demonstrations on 19 April. On 25 April university professors marched in Seoul in support of the students. Under pressure that included a unanimous vote of the National Assembly and the views of the United States government, Rhee resigned on 27 April 1960 and went into exile in Hawaii.
900.explanation: A president who controlled the police, the ruling party and a powerful foreign alliance could not survive once students and their teachers stood together against him.
900.tie_back: The kural says that even those with boundless support cannot escape when people of outstanding worth are roused against them, and Rhee's support melted away in weeks.
900._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: it shows vast support failing a ruler, though the force that toppled him was a mass movement rather than a few great individuals.
